title: The Council Meeting

pages.text:
*Garden Log, Day 234: Speaking: yes. Shaking: also yes.*

The Council Chamber smelled of cold wood and floor wax. The ceiling was high enough to hang a kite from, if you had a very long string. Twelve wooden chairs faced a curved desk where the clerk sat behind a glass partition. He looked at the room, then at the floor, then at the room again.

We had taken the number 4 bus. It had been full. Mrs. Ilves had brought a basket of tomatoes so red they looked like alarm lights. Theo held a pear branch that had fallen off the Autumn wall. And in a shoebox, with a towel and a bit of lettuce, was Gherkin. The clerk’s eyes slid over the tortoise as if it were a smudge on the table.

Ms. Vandermeer walked in last. She wore a grey suit and carried a laptop bag. She stopped. She looked at the tomatoes. She looked at the tortoise. She looked at the forty people standing in the back, most of them wearing the same kind of coat. Her lips moved, but no sound came out. She plugged in her laptop and started typing.
pages.image: A cold high-ceilinged council chamber with wood panels; a crowd of residents stands at the back, one holding a red tomato, another holding Gherkin, a small hat-sized tortoise, in a shoebox, while Ms. Vandermeer, a neat woman in a grey suit, looks bewildered at the front desk

pages.text:
Mr. Osei stood up, holding his cap in his hands and turning the brim over and under while the room went quiet, that specific silence that happens when a teacher stops talking to see if you are actually listening.

"My name is Kwame Osei," he said, his voice low but filling the whole space. "Thirty years ago, I made a garden on the land behind the bins. With my wife, Ada."

He looked at his cap, then at the clerk.

"It fed half the estate. We had tomatoes. We had beans. We had peace." He paused, and the silence stretched out like a taffy pull. "I closed it because I was sad. I was wrong."

He sat down, and for a second there was nothing. Then the room erupted. Mrs. Ilves clapped, Theo cheered, and even the clerk looked up. I looked at Mr. Osei, who was wiping his hands on his overalls, but his shoulders were straight for the first time I had ever seen.
pages.image: A tall man in blue overalls stands at a podium in a wood-paneled room, holding a cap; behind him, a crowd of residents claps, and a small tortoise sits in a shoebox on a table in the foreground.

pages.text:
Then it was my turn.

My knees had turned to that marshmallow fluff I hate, and my mouth felt like the back of a shampoo bottle, all dry and useless. The speech was written on the back of my hand, a tiny scrawl that blurred when I tried to read it. My heart was thumping against my ribs. I walked to the front, where the microphone stood up at me, impossibly tall, so I had to stand on my tiptoes just to see its face.

I looked at the clerk, then at Ms. Vandermeer, then up at the high ceiling, counting the tiles because counting helps when you are terrified.

"My name is Sana Haddad," I said, and my voice wobbled. "I am eleven. And I am shaking."

The room laughed. It was not a cruel laugh; it was a soft, warm sound. I looked at them, and the knot in my chest loosened, and I found the rest of my sentence hiding in that laughter.

"I am here to talk about a garden," I said. "And I am still shaking."
pages.image: A thin girl with round glasses and a denim jacket stands on tiptoes at a podium, holding a small piece of paper; a crowd of smiling neighbors watches from behind, and a neat woman in a suit listens with interest.

pages.text:
"I planted a seed in that garden," I said, my voice steadier than my legs. "It took sixty days to flower. I watched it every day. I measured it. I waited for it."

I took a breath, trying to remember how lungs work without shaking.

"You cannot see a garden from a chart. You cannot see it on a screen. Your paper calls it 'derelict land.' It is not. It is the opposite. It is alive."

I looked at Ms. Vandermeer. She had stopped typing, and her fingers were still on the keys, hovering like they didn't know what to do next. She was looking at me.

"I invite you to come and look," I said. "Not with a map. With your hands. Say one true thing. And see what happens."

I stepped back from the microphone, which felt much less tall now that I wasn't standing on my tiptoes. My legs felt like they had been filled with cold jelly, but I was standing upright. The room was silent. I could hear the rain tapping on the glass above the windows. It sounded like applause, but slower. Much slower.
pages.image: A girl in a denim jacket stands confidently at a podium, gesturing toward a woman in a grey suit; the wood-paneled room is quiet, with rain visible on the high windows in the background.

pages.text:
They did not cheer, and nobody stood up to clap. Instead, the room erupted into a debate about "risk assessments" and "community engagement," terms that sounded like video game loading screens that never finished loading. I stood by the wall, counting the cracks in the concrete floor while they discussed "trial periods" for forty minutes.

Finally, the clerk read the decision aloud. The land sale was postponed for one year, and a formal site visit would be arranged. It was not a victory, nor was it a defeat. It was just a pause, a long, held breath.

I felt dizzy. For the first time in my life, I was grateful for the words themselves, and even more so for the wait they promised. I looked toward the door, knowing I was going back to the garden.

"Not yet," I whispered.

And for once, it was enough.
